title: When the Undertow Sings
premise: Juniper Ravensworth, a bridge inspector whose own marriage has corroded like the spans they assess, returns to their decaying childhood home when it goes up for auction, forced to confront the mother they have spent twenty years resenting. Sifting through old photographs, letters, and the house's failing bones, Juniper discovers their mother's sacrifices were hidden inside the very silences that felt like abandonment, and that their spouse, Marisol, has been quietly carrying her own unspoken grief. As the auction date and demolition permit converge, Juniper must choose between preserving the house as a monument to grievance or letting it fall while salvaging what is true: forgiveness, and a marriage worth rebuilding. The book ends at the demolition itself, where Juniper, hand in hand with Marisol, lets the house come down and finally hears the undertow of the past as a song rather than a warning.
about_author: Isandro Sterling is the pen name of a former civil engineer who spent a decade inspecting coastal bridges before turning to fiction full-time. Their work examines how structures — steel, houses, marriages — bear weight, fail slowly, and sometimes forgive.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Juniper, in their POV, inspects a failing coastal bridge, measuring its movement the way they've stopped measuring anything at home. A terse exchange with Marisol over breakfast reveals a marriage of polite cohabitation. The emotional beat: numbness mistaken for stability.

chapters.title: Notice of Sale
chapters.summary: A certified letter announces the auction of the Ravensworth house on Gull Point — the childhood home Juniper fled at nineteen and never returned to. Marisol insists on going; Juniper resists. POV Juniper. Emotional beat: dread disguised as indifference.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV: she watches Juniper sleep and admits she's been a tenant in her own marriage since a miscarriage three years ago that neither of them named. She packs the car anyway, hoping the trip will force a reckoning. Emotional beat: quiet, desperate hope.

chapters.title: Gull Point
chapters.summary: The couple arrives at the sagging house ahead of the auction open house. Juniper walks rooms that feel both foreign and carved into their body. A neighbor, Odette, recognizes them and says, 'Your mother kept your room exactly.' POV Juniper. Beat: vertigo of return.

chapters.title: What the Water Kept
chapters.summary: Juniper finds their childhood bedroom untouched, including a photograph of their mother, Ruth, younger and laughing — a stranger. Marisol finds a locked cedar chest in the attic. POV Marisol. Beat: the first crack in Juniper's grievance.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: Bidders swarm the house; a developer, Callum Voss, plans demolition for a resort. Juniper, on impulse and against every plan, wins the auction with money they cannot spare. POV Juniper. Beat: reckless inheritance — owning what you never wanted.

chapters.title: Buyer's Remorse
chapters.summary: Back home, Juniper and Marisol fight about the money, and the fight detonates into the real one — the miscarriage, the silence, the years of polite distance. POV Marisol. Beat: the marriage's hidden fracture exposed to air.

chapters.title: Load Rating
chapters.summary: Juniper returns to the bridge job but can't concentrate, seeing corrosion everywhere as metaphor. A near-miss with a fraying cable shakes them. POV Juniper. Beat: the realization that neglect, not malice, destroys things.

chapters.title: The Cedar Chest
chapters.summary: Weekend at the house: Marisol pries open the chest and finds Ruth's unmailed letters — dozens addressed to Juniper, never sent. She reads one and hides the rest, unsure Juniper is ready. POV Marisol. Beat: the burden of knowing.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Marisol begins leaving letters where Juniper will find them, one at a time. The first reveals Ruth's diagnosis — early-onset dementia — the year Juniper left, and her choice to push them away so they wouldn't watch her disappear. POV Juniper. Beat: grief reframing rage.

chapters.title: Odette's Testimony
chapters.summary: Odette, over tea, tells the truth of Ruth's final decade: the woman who forgot her own name but never Juniper's, walking to the point every evening 'to watch for the ferry you'd come home on.' POV Juniper. Beat: the stranger in the photographs becomes human.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Voss's lawyers confirm the sale is final; demolition in eight weeks. Juniper, now the owner, must either restore a house they can't afford or sign the demolition order themselves. POV Marisol. Beat: inheritance as a trap and an invitation.

chapters.title: Scaffolding
chapters.summary: Juniper begins repairing the house with their own hands — an inspector who finally inspects something they love. Marisol joins without being asked. They work in a silence that is, for once, companionable. POV Juniper. Beat: labor as apology and prayer.

chapters.title: The Room at the End of the Hall
chapters.summary: They discover a sealed room: a nursery Ruth prepared in secret the year before her diagnosis, filled with unfinished things — a quilt, a mobile, letters to a grandchild she anticipated. POV Marisol. Beat: Ruth's hope outliving her memory.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: A storm floods the point; Juniper and Marisol race to save the letters and are caught in the rising water, nearly drowned, saved by clinging to the porch rail together. POV Juniper. Beat: the past literally tries to pull them under; they hold on to each other.

chapters.title: What the Storm Took
chapters.summary: Half the letters are destroyed. Marisol confesses she read them first, and Juniper — instead of raging — forgives her, understanding secrecy as love's clumsy guardian. POV Marisol. Beat: the marriage's first real repair.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: The final surviving letter, dated weeks before Ruth's death, asks forgiveness not for the silence but for teaching Juniper that love means hiding. Juniper reads it aloud to Marisol in the ruined nursery. POV Juniper. Beat: forgiveness begins as understanding.

chapters.title: Voss's Offer
chapters.summary: Voss returns with a generous buyout, enough to erase their debts and start over anywhere. Juniper is tempted — a clean escape from the whole painful inheritance. POV Marisol. Beat: the temptation to skip the hard work of grief.

chapters.title: What We Keep
chapters.summary: Juniper declines the offer but signs the demolition order — choosing to keep the letters, the quilt, and each other, and to let the house go. Marisol, stunned, realizes Juniper has finally chosen ownership over tenancy in their own life. POV Juniper. Beat: the costly, freeing choice.

chapters.title: Demolition Day
chapters.summary: Neighbors gather. Juniper and Marisol stand hand in hand as the excavator swings. Juniper speaks a few words of farewell to the mother in the photographs — no longer a stranger. POV Juniper. Beat: climax — grief and release in the same breath.

chapters.title: The Sound It Made
chapters.summary: Afterward, walking the empty point, Juniper finally hears what Ruth heard every evening: the undertow's low rhythm against the rocks, steady as a heartbeat, like a song that was always singing for them. POV Marisol, watching Juniper listen. Beat: transfiguration.

chapters.title: Load-Bearing
chapters.summary: Months later, Juniper inspects a bridge and signs off on repairs rather than condemnation — believing things can be mended. At home, Marisol hangs the finished quilt; the nursery letters go into a box labeled for the future. POV Juniper. Beat: resolution — inheritance reclaimed as love.
